paragraphs.text: We may safely pray the same, when oppressed with calumnies and false accusations, as now David was by Saul’s sycophants, or, as others think, when he was in great heaviness, and even heart sick; after that Amnon had defiled Tamar, and Absalom had slain Amnon; his disaffected subjects, such as Shimei, insulted over him, and said, it was just upon him for the matter of Uriah, and other miscarriages; which they wrongfully charged him with. See a promise in this case, Isa 49:21.
paragraphs.anchor: Plead my cause, O Lord

paragraphs.text: Or, devour them that devour me; for in Niphal only it signifieth to fight.
paragraphs.anchor: Fight against them, &c.

paragraphs.text: Jehovah is a man of war, Exo 15:3, and so he is here stirred up to harness himself; not that he needeth weapons defensive, as here, or offensive, as Psa 35:3, for he can destroy his enemies, solo nutu ac flatu, with a nod, or a blast; but this is spoken after the manner of men, and for our better apprehension of God’s readiness to relieve his distressed ones.
paragraphs.anchor: Take hold of shield and buckler

paragraphs.text: viz. That thy contending and appearing for me may appear to be sufficient and glorious.
paragraphs.anchor: Draw out also the spear

paragraphs.text: Heb. And stop, viz. the doors, as Gen 19:6; Gen 19:10 2Ki 6:32, lest the malcontents come in and kill me. Or, shut me up from my persecutors, that they find me not; like as, afterwards, God hid Jeremiah and Baruch, when sought for to the slaughter.
paragraphs.anchor: And stop the way

paragraphs.text: Facito ut haec animula te sibi testantem audiat, &c. Inwardly persuade my heart to firm affiance in thee, amidst all mine afflictions.
paragraphs.anchor: Say unto my soul, I am thy salvation

paragraphs.text: Here David beginneth his imprecations; which yet non maledicens dixit sed vaticinantis more praedixit, saith Theodoret, he doth not utter as cursing, but as prophesying rather. If we shall at any time take upon us thus to imprecate (as we may in some cases), we must see to it, first, that our cause be good. Secondly, that we do it not out of private revenge; but merely for the glory of God. Thirdly, ut ne voculam quidem nisi nobis praeeunte Dei, non carnis, spiritu effundamus, that we utter not a syllable this way but by the guidance of God’s good Spirit.
paragraphs.anchor: Let them be confounded and put to shame

paragraphs.text: Facti sint a corde suo fugitivi, let them fly before their own consciences, restless and uncertain whither to turn themselves.
paragraphs.anchor: Let them be as chaff

paragraphs.text: It may be understood both of the evil angels and of the good, ready at God’s command to do execution upon his enemies. Chaff driven before the wind may rest against a wall; but where shall they rest who are chased by an angel? "Where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?" 1Pe 4:18. Surely nowhere.
paragraphs.anchor: And let the angel of the Lord chase them

paragraphs.text: Heb. Darkness and slipperiness. If a man have neither light nor firm footing, and a fierce enemy at his heels, what shift can he make for himself? The word rendered slippery is of a double form (like that libbi secharchar, my heart panteth or beateth about, throbbeth, Psa 38:10), to increase the signfication. See Jer 23:12. The soul of a wicked man is in a sling, 1Sa 25:29, violently tossed about.
paragraphs.anchor: Let their way be dark and slippery

paragraphs.text: The wicked are so acted and agitated by the devil, their task master, that, though they have no cause to work mischief to the saints, yet they must do it; the old enmity, Gen 3:15, still worketh; but this rendereth their destruction certiorem et celeriorem, more sure and more swift.
paragraphs.anchor: For without cause have they hid for me, &c.

paragraphs.text: i.e. Upon the whole rabble of them, as if they were all but one man. Or else he striketh at some chieftain among them. Let his destruction be as sudden as signal.
paragraphs.anchor: Let destruction come upon him unawares

paragraphs.text: This was what he aimed at in his foregoing imprecations, viz. the glory and praise of God, and not his own wreaking his spleen upon his enemies.
paragraphs.anchor: And my soul shall be joyful in the Lord

paragraphs.text: Not my soul only, but my body also shall join in this joyful acclamation; yea, my bones shall say, &c., that is, whatsoever strength and vigour is in me, it shall be spent in celebrating thy praises. Or, although I have nothing left me but skin and bones, so poor am I grown, yet I will not be wanting to the work.
paragraphs.anchor: All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like unto thee?

paragraphs.text: So they did afterward against the Lord Christ and sundry of his faithful servants, as St Paul, Athanasius, Eustathius, bishop of Antioch (falsely accused of adultery, and deposed, about the end of Constantine the Great’s reign), Cranmer, charged with adultery, heresy, and treason; Philpot, with parricide; Latimer, with sedition; whereof he was so innocent, that he feared not to say in a sermon before the king, As for sedition, for aught that I know, methinks I should not need Christ, if I may so say.
paragraphs.anchor: False witnesses did rise up

paragraphs.text: Such as whereof I was not only innocent, but ignorant also. The Hebrew is, They asked me, and so would have, by cunningly contrived questions, made me mine own accuser.
paragraphs.anchor: They laid to my charge things that I knew not

paragraphs.text: To render good for evil is divine, good for good is human, evil for evil is brutish; but evil for good is devilish.
paragraphs.anchor: They rewarded me evil for good

paragraphs.text: i.e. To the depriving me of that life which I have so often hazarded to save theirs. Intentant caedem (Kimchi). Or, this their devilish dealing with me, erat mihi quasi mors amarum, was as bitter as death to me.
paragraphs.anchor: To the spoiling of my soul

paragraphs.text: i.e. Any way afflicted, when they ailed anything.
paragraphs.anchor: But as for me, when they were sick

paragraphs.text: I put myself in mourners’ habit; Incedebam atratus, to testify my good affection toward them.
paragraphs.anchor: My clothing was sachcloth

paragraphs.text: In die designate, in a solemn day set apart for the purpose; as the ð with a patach showeth (Kimehi). Ieiunium est humilitas mentis, miserationis expensa, charitatis illecebra, allevamentum infirmitatis, alimentum salutis, saith Ambrose, Fasting is the affliction of the soul, the cost of compassion, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: I humbled my soul with fasting

paragraphs.text: And my prayer returned into mine own bosom] i.e. Though they had no benefit by it, yet myself had; for no faithful prayer is ineffectual; like Jonathan’s bow, it never returned empty, 2Sa 1:22. I received the fruit of my prayers for them upon my bosom.
My brother a thousand times. This was much to do to an enemy; but possibly all this might be before they fell out.
paragraphs.anchor: I behaved myself as though he had been, &c.

paragraphs.text: The mother is usually most dearly beloved, and not without cause, as having been ante partum onerosa, in partu dolorosa, post partum laboriosa (Kimchi). Or, as a suckling crieth in the loss of his nurse.
paragraphs.anchor: I bowed down heavily, as one that mourneth, &c.

paragraphs.text: Heb. in my halting; when through weakness I could not but halt before my best friends, as we say. Morbus est sic dictus quia incedere nequit nisi cum doloro quasi claudicando (Aben-Ezra).
paragraphs.anchor: But in mine adversity

paragraphs.text: Claudi congregati sunt, et secundum claudicationem meam claudicabant, ut me deriderent, so the Syriac senseth it. They halted, as I did, by way of derision; but they should have known, first, that mocking is catching, as we say. Cicero confesseth that while he laughed at one Hircus, a very ridiculous man, he became as bad almost himself: Dum illum rideo, pene factus sum ille (Epist. 9, lib. 2). Secondly, that such cruel mockings are grievous sins, and such as God will severely punish. Some render it the smiters, that is, the tongue smiters, as Jer 18:18. Others, the smitten, that is, the abjects, the vile persons: the basest can mock, as did Tobiah the servant, Neh 2:19, and those pests, Psa 1:1.
paragraphs.anchor: Yea, the abjects gathered themselves together

paragraphs.text: Or, such as I knew not, took no notice of, they were so base. See the like, Job 30:8.
paragraphs.anchor: And I knew not

paragraphs.text: sc. With their tongues, as dogs toss and tear carrion with their teeth, Scindunt illud quod reparare nequeunt, non per pcenitentiam, saith Kimchi. They tear that which they cannot make good again, no, not by repentance, viz. my good name. Or, they rent, sc. their garments, as if they had been very sorry for me, as Gen 37:36 Job 2:12. This they did, as Austin speaketh, simulatione miseriae, non compassione misericordiae, out of deep dissimulation.
paragraphs.anchor: They did tear me

paragraphs.text: Cum sannionibus placentae vel cibi, with hypocritical mockers for a cake or dainties. There is an elegance in the original, which showeth it to be proverbial, and cannot be translated R. Solomon telleth us here, that they who delighted in flatteries gave their flatterers cakes baked with honey, to make them the more to flatter them. Solomon telleth of some that will transgress for a piece of bread, Pro 28:21. So those parasitic prophets, Eze 13:19. Or, I am made their table talk, as Hos 7:8, scornfully deriding me at their feasts and in their cups, Mensarii scurrae.
paragraphs.anchor: With hypocritical mockers in feasts

paragraphs.text: i.e. Carry thyself as a spectator of my miseries and a tolerator of mine enemies, those architects of mine afflictions.
paragraphs.anchor: Lord, how long wilt thou look on?

paragraphs.text: i.e. Their snares and ambushes, whereby they seek to destroy me.
paragraphs.anchor: Rescue my soul from their destructions

paragraphs.text: {See Trapp on "Psa 22:20"}
paragraphs.anchor: My darling from the lions

paragraphs.text: For example’s sake to others; for Magnates magnetos. Act 18:8, when Crispus, the chief ruler of the synagogue, believed, many of the Corinthians believed also. Great men are the looking glasses of the country, according to which most men dress themselves; many eyes are upon them; they had need, therefore, to be exact, for they are sure to be exemplary.
paragraphs.anchor: I will give thee thanks in the great congregation

paragraphs.text: Which is the gesture of a malicious scoffer, Pro 6:13; Pro 10:10. Ne amarulenter ludificentur me (Trem.).
paragraphs.anchor: Neither let them wink with the eye

paragraphs.text: Which yet God doth to his people, Psa 85:9, and that is their comfort. "I am for peace," saith David elsewhere, "but when I speak, they are for war," Psa 120:7.
paragraphs.anchor: For they speak not peace

paragraphs.text: i.e. Against myself, and such as I am, who study to be quiet and to do our own business, 1Th 4:11, affecting rather quietness from the world than acquaintance with it.
paragraphs.anchor: Against the quiet of the land

paragraphs.text: As if the very banks of blasphemy had been broken down.
paragraphs.anchor: They opened their mouth

paragraphs.text: Eye for eyes, unless we would say that all the wicked are so conjoined, that they may seem to have but one eye, heart, head, &c., and then they say, as Hannibal did, when he saw a ditch full of man’s blood, O formosum spectaculum! O gallant sight! O rem regiam! as Valesus said, when he had slain three hundred Protestants.
paragraphs.anchor: Our eye hath seen

paragraphs.text: This answereth to that before, Psa 35:21. Our eye hath seen it, as Aben Ezra observeth. So doth
paragraphs.anchor: This thou hast seen, O Lord

paragraphs.text: To that they opened their mouth wide against me. Ibid.
paragraphs.anchor: Keep not silence

paragraphs.text: This is the same in effect with the beginning of the psalm; to show his ardour and intention of affection.
paragraphs.anchor: Stir up thyself and awake

paragraphs.text: i.e. For the honour of thy justice, wherein else thou art likely to suffer.
paragraphs.anchor: According to thy righteousness

paragraphs.text: For I quarter arms, as I may so say, with thee, Lord; and my disgrace will reflect upon thee.
paragraphs.anchor: And let them not rejoice over me

paragraphs.text: Heb. Ah, ah, my soul; that is, our desire; we are voti compotes.
paragraphs.anchor: Ah, so would we have it

paragraphs.text: As swine do swill or ravenous beasts their prey.
paragraphs.anchor: We have swallowed them up

paragraphs.text: They shall so; and this prayer against the Church’s enemies shall still speak effectually.
paragraphs.anchor: Let them be ashamed, &c.

paragraphs.text: He concludeth with hearty prayer for the Church, as he doth in various other psalms.
paragraphs.anchor: Let them shout for joy, &c.

paragraphs.text: Though perhaps they dare do no more than inwardly favour it and by their prayers to God promote it.
paragraphs.anchor: That favour thy righteous cause

paragraphs.text: Let them have continual cause to praise God for this sweet property, that he delighteth in his people’s prosperity, and afflicts them not from his heart, nor grieveth the children of men, but for their greatest good, Lam 3:35.
paragraphs.anchor: Let them say continually, &c.

paragraphs.text: I do solemnly promise that thy praises shall never die on my hand, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: And my tongue, &c.
